+ Physical-spatial: Breaking Formation — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The mirror is a lie. It shows me a body I don’t recognize, wrapped in sweat-soaked black cotton, standing in a line of seventeen other trainees who all breathe on the same count. My reflection is late. Every time I look, I’m a half-beat behind the boy to my left—a kid from Busan who can pivot on a dime without breaking his center. My center is a wreck. It’s a bonfire, not a fulcrum. “Again.” Instructor Hwang’s voice doesn’t carry. It cuts. He stands at the front of the studio, a man in wire-rimmed glasses and a charcoal turtleneck, holding a folding hand fan against his thigh. He hasn’t raised it in twenty minutes. That means we keep moving. That means he hasn’t found the exact second he wants to punish. I reset to the opening mark—feet together, arms strapped to my sides like I’m in a coffin. The music starts. A synthetic pulse, 128 BPM, clean as a scalpel. The first eight counts are a slow head isolation: chin forward, chin left, chin right, chin down. It’s supposed to look like a machine calibrating. I do it. My neck grinds against the memory of a headspin I threw last week on the corner of Atlantic and Nostrand, where the asphalt chews through sneakers and the crowd doesn’t clap—they nod. One nod is worth a stadium. Count nine. We break into a shoulder roll sequence. Left shoulder rolls back, right shoulder rolls forward, torso stays locked like a mannequin. The kid from Busan is a ghost of precision. His shoulders move independent of his ribs. Mine hitch. My left shoulder wants to drop into a wave, wants to let the momentum travel down my arm and into a ripple. That’s how I speak. That’s how I survived. But here, a wave is a mistake. The girl behind me—Seoyeon, I think—pulls a sharp breath through her teeth. She can feel my wrongness like a flat tire on a highway. We hit the first major transition. Feet slide into a V-step, then a body roll from the chest down to the knees, then a sharp pop of the ribcage on the downbeat. It’s a lock-and-pose move. I’ve seen it in K-pop videos a thousand times. I’ve mocked it, honestly. Called it factory dancing. Now the factory owns my ligaments. On the pop, my spine tries to freestyle. It wants to undulate, to breathe. The choreography demands a *stop*. A full-body punctuation mark. My ribs lock a millisecond late. The result is a wobble—a tremor that travels from my solar plexus to my fingertips. In the mirror, I look like a bridge about to collapse. Hwang’s fan snaps shut. The sound is a gunshot in the treated air. We freeze. Seventeen bodies, mid-pose. My right arm is extended at a forty-five-degree angle, palm flat, fingers spread. The kid next to me has his arm at exactly forty-seven degrees. I can see the difference in the reflection. It’s three degrees of failure. Hwang walks. His footsteps are silent. He stops behind me. I don’t turn my head. I’ve learned that much. Looking at him is an invitation. “Your spine is a column,” he says. His English is precise, clipped. He doesn’t need to yell. “Not a snake. You are not a snake. You are a building. A building does not sway.” I want to say: *Buildings fall. Snakes survive.* But I keep my jaw locked. My jaw is a column. He walks to the front. “From the top. The shoulder roll sequence. You will do it until your shoulders forget they have bones.” The music restarts. I do it. Again. Again. My left shoulder burns. The kid from Busan is still perfect. Seoyeon is still silent. I am still three degrees off, but now it’s two. Improvement. Or exhaustion. I think about the scholarship. The letter that arrived in a thick cream envelope, the one my mother framed above the stove. *Full tuition. Housing. A pathway to debut.* The woman who handed it to me at the community center had a handshake like wet paper. She said I had “raw potential.” She didn’t say I’d have to kill the thing that made me raw. We hit the chorus. The choreography breaks into a high-energy sequence—a four-count of footwork that looks like a military drill. Left foot crosses behind, right foot kicks, left foot returns, right foot stomps. Repeat. Then a spin. Then a drop to one knee, arms crossed over the chest, head down. I know footwork. I was born in footwork. On my block, footwork is a conversation. You slide, you jab, you sweep, you fake. You answer a challenge with a pattern. But this—this is not a conversation. This is a script. Every toe placement is plotted. My muscle memory tries to help. It tries to add a glide. My left foot crosses behind, and my instinct says *drag the back toe for style*. I do it. It’s a fraction of a second. It throws off my right kick. The kick lands soft. The stomp lands late. The fan snaps again. “Stop.” We freeze. I’m on one knee. My head is down. I can see the sweat dripping off my nose onto the polished floor. It makes a dark spot. I watch it spread. Hwang crouches in front of me. His face is level with mine. He doesn’t look angry. He looks curious. That’s worse. “Where did you learn to move like that?” I don’t know how to answer. *The street* sounds like a cliché. *The block* sounds like a threat. *My body* sounds like an excuse. “Outside,” I say. He nods slowly. “Outside has no beat. Outside has no line. Outside is a crowd. This—” he taps the floor with his fan, “—is a stage. A stage has borders. You must learn to live inside the border.” He stands. He walks back to his spot. He doesn’t snap his fan open. He holds it closed. “One more time. The chorus. From the top. And this time, do not help the choreography. It does not need your help.” The music starts. I feel the beat in my teeth. I feel the rhythm in my wrists. I feel the old language flooding my veins, begging to be spoken. The footwork begins. Left foot crosses. My instinct screams *glide*. I stop it. I lock the glide. My foot lands flat. The kick is sharp. The stomp is on time. I spin. I drop. I cross my arms. I put my head down. I am a building. The building wants to dance. I stay still. For one count. Two. The music moves on without me. The others rise. I rise with them, a half-beat behind, but this time I don’t panic. I watch my reflection. It’s still a stranger. But the stranger is learning to stand still. Hwang opens his fan. He doesn’t snap it. He waves it, gently, once, like a dismissal. Or a breath. I don’t know if I’ve passed or failed. I only know that my spine is straight, and my fists are clenched inside my sleeves, and somewhere in the marrow of my bones, the snake is coiling, waiting for the moment the building cracks.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, tightly controlled piece that fulfills nearly every instruction. The first-person voice is distinct and consistent: street-inflected, wry, observant, with a strong metaphorical spine (snake vs. building, mirror as lie). Physical coherence is excellent—each move (head isolations, shoulder rolls, V-step, footwork sequence) is tracked spatially and temporally, and the "three degrees of failure" detail is a superb concrete image of technical shortfall. The collision of street and commercial vocabularies is rendered through specific terminology (popping, waving, gliding, toe drag, isolations) and through muscle memory betrayals that are shown kinetically rather than explained. Culture shock and class anxiety are present but slightly underdeveloped—the mother framing the letter, the community center handshake are good touches, but the class dimension is thinner than the technical one. The decision point (conform vs. rebel) is handled with genuine ambiguity: the narrator conforms for one pass but the ending's coiled snake preserves the tension, avoiding a cheap resolution. Hwang is a nicely economical character—curious rather than cruel, with the fan as an effective recurring device. Minor flaws: some aphorisms ("One nod is worth a stadium") flirt with over-polish; the Busan kid and Seoyeon remain props; the "three degrees" of arm angle is technically implausible to perceive visually, though it works as subjective perception. Dialogue is sparse but sharp and character-revealing. The prose is disciplined, never purple, and the pacing never meanders. Emotionally it engages through restraint and physicality rather than sentiment—which is the right call. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 64.8
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The air in the Court of the Dreaming tasted of ozone and forgotten sorrows. The vast hall, a cathedral of obsidian and starlight, held a gallery of murmuring phantoms. At the high bench, Dream of the Endless sat, a figure of pale, sharp-angled stillness, his eyes twin galaxies of bored contempt. “The Court will come to order,” boomed the Bailiff, a creature of shifting shadow and stone. “The case of *First Love* versus *Mora* is now in session. Let the petitioner approach.” A rosy-cheeked entity shuffled forward. He was dressed in a slightly-too-tight corduroy jacket, clutching a sheaf of parchment. His name was, simply, First Love. He looked like he might cry. “Your Lordship,” First Love began, his voice a wobbly tenor. “I have been wronged. For six months, I have curated a recurring dreamscape for the human child, Max. A field of wildflowers. A girl named Chloe. The scent of cut grass and possibility. The almost-kiss. It was a masterpiece of adolescent yearning.” “Yes,” Dream said, his voice a low, cold river. “I am familiar with the template. It is a common one. What is your grievance?” “She *ruined* it!” First Love pointed a trembling finger at the defendant’s table. Mora was a stooped, grey-skinned thing with lank, oily hair and a knowing smile. She perched on her chair like a gargoyle at a tea party. She offered a small, apologetic wave. “Go on,” Dream said. “Last Tuesday,” First Love continued, his cheeks flushing, “Max fell asleep. The dream began perfectly. The field. The golden hour. Chloe giggled, she mounted him playfully, her hair brushing his face. And then—” He choked. “*Then* she dissolved. Her features melted. She grew heavy. Her breath became *cold*. She sat on his chest, her face a grinning, beautiful horror, and she *fed*.” Mora cleared her throat. “Objection. ‘Fed’ is such a strong word. I prefer ‘subtle respiration reclamation’.” “Silence,” Dream said. He turned his starry gaze upon her. “Mora. You are charged with territorial dream subversion. How do you plead?” “Guilty, I suppose,” she said, shrugging. “But with an explanation.” “Which is?” She leaned forward, her voice a rasp of dry leaves. “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know? The boy’s dreamscape was *lush*. Ripe. All that fluttering hope, that sweet, useless tension. It’s wasted on an almost-kiss. That’s just *advertising*. I’m in the business of *product*. I turn that soft, sighing terror into a protein-rich nightmare. It’s practical. It’s sustainable.” “You have turned a formative romantic experience into a respiratory assault,” Dream said, his tone flat. “It’s still formative!” Mora insisted. “He wakes up terrified, yes, but also… confused. Aroused. I’ve added *layers*. The girl he likes is now also a monster who steals his breath. That’s a metaphor for intimacy if I’ve ever heard one. I’ve improved his dream. I’ve made it *interesting*.” First Love sputtered. “She sits on his chest! She feeds on his breath! He’s waking up with sleep paralysis!” “Builds character,” Mora muttered. Dream’s fingers, long and white, tapped the arm of his throne. A faint, almost imperceptible irritation flickered in the depths of his eyes. “This is a territorial dispute. The dreamscape was established. It is not a shared resource.” “With respect, my Lord,” Mora said, “the dreamscape was *underutilized*. It was a single-use, single-emotion property. I have diversified the portfolio. I have introduced a recurring revenue stream. The boy now has a dream that is both terrifying and arousing. That’s a premium product.” The gallery murmured. A few phantoms nodded. “The boy is losing sleep,” First Love said weakly. “He’s gaining *experience*,” Mora countered. Dream raised a hand. The hall fell silent. He looked at the two entities, his expression unreadable. “The dreamscape is, by law, the property of the first entity to establish a recurring narrative within it. First Love has a clear claim. However,” he paused, a flicker of something—amusement?—passing across his features, “the Court acknowledges the principle of *use it or lose it*.” First Love’s face fell. “The dreamscape has been altered,” Dream continued. “The boy now associates Chloe with both desire and dread. This is a complex emotional state. It is, in its own way, more potent than the original.” Mora grinned, revealing too many teeth. “Therefore,” Dream said, “the Court finds in favor of… neither party.” A gasp rippled through the hall. “The dreamscape is hereby placed in receivership. It will be managed by a neutral third party. One who understands the delicate balance between sweetness and terror.” He snapped his fingers. A figure stepped from the shadows. It was a small, wizened creature in a wrinkled suit, clutching a ledger. It was the Court’s official dream adjudicator. “Recorder,” Dream said, “you will oversee the dreamscape. You will ensure that for every two nights of First Love’s gentle yearning, there is one night of Mora’s breath-stealing horror. The boy will have a confused, unstable, but ultimately *richer* dream life.” First Love looked devastated. Mora looked triumphant. “One more thing,” Dream said, his voice dropping to a near-whisper. “The boy, Max. He is currently dreaming of a math exam. He is naked. The exam is in ancient Sumerian. The proctor is a giant, disapproving owl.” First Love and Mora stared at him. “That,” Dream said, a ghost of a smile touching his lips, “is what happens when you waste my time with petty squabbles. The Court is adjourned.” The Bailiff’s voice boomed one last time. “The Court will now hear the case of *Morpheus versus the Principle of Tedium*. All rise.” Dream was already gone, leaving behind only the faint scent of night and the sound of a distant, mocking laugh.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent courtroom farce with the requested beats: Mora's "a girl's gotta eat" defense, First Love's wounded craftsmanship, Dream's irritation, and a resolution involving Dream's mischief (the Sumerian owl exam dream is a nice touch of petty spite). The corporate-satire angle on Mora ("recurring revenue stream," "premium product") is the strongest comedic vein and lands with dry, understated wit. Dream's "use it or lose it" ruling and the receivership compromise is a reasonably clever legal-farcical resolution. Weaknesses: the prose leans on stock descriptors ("twin galaxies of bored contempt," "a low, cold river," "rasp of dry leaves") — serviceable but occasionally clichéd. There is a fair amount of telling ("He looked like he might cry," "First Love looked devastated. Mora looked triumphant"), and the emotional states of the gallery and parties are frequently narrated rather than dramatized. The dialogue is functional and sometimes funny, but several exchanges are on-the-nose, and Mora's voice occasionally drifts between folk-horror rasp and LinkedIn strategist without full control. The ending's final flourish ("Morpheus versus the Principle of Tedium") is a decent absurdist button, though the "mocking laugh" is a slightly overwrought exit. Character nuance is thin: First Love is a one-note sad artisan, Mora a one-note pragmatist; Dream himself is the most textured presence. The piece adheres well to the prompt's constraints (dark comedy, understated, Dream's irritation, mischief in resolution) and maintains tonal consistency throughout. It is coherent and briskly paced, never meandering, but also plays things safe — the structure is predictable courtroom beats enlivened by jokes rather than any genuine surprise or emotional depth. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 73.2
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The moon hangs swollen and red over the Carpathian foothills, a bleeding wound in the fabric of night. The air smells of damp earth and pine resin, and beneath it, something older—copper and grave soil. Yennefer of Vengerberg stands at the edge of a ruined watchtower, her black dress whipping around her ankles. She has been tracking the source of the magical disturbance for three days. The local villagers speak of a *strzyga*, a vampire of the old blood, but their descriptions are too precise, too theatrical. A man in red. A hat with a wide brim. Laughter that echoes wrong. She does not believe in coincidence. The wolves fall silent. Yennefer’s fingers curl, a spell already threading between them, when she hears the footsteps—deliberate, unhurried, the cadence of someone who has never needed to run. “A sorceress,” a voice says from the shadows. “Out so late. Did you lose your broom?” He steps into the moonlight. The coat is absurd, a slash of crimson against the monochrome night. The hat casts his face in shadow, but she sees the grin—too wide, too white. The orange glasses are an affectation, a mockery of human fashion. Yennefer does not flinch. “I lost my patience. I thought I might find it here.” Alucard laughs. It is not a pleasant sound. It crawls along her spine like something alive. “Charming,” he says. “The little mage has teeth.” He is not what she expected. She has encountered vampires before—brutish things, driven by hunger and little else. This one stands with the coiled stillness of a predator who has never known fear. His presence presses against her magical senses like a wall of cold iron. “I am Yennefer of Vengerberg.” “I know who you are.” He tilts his head. “I smelled you from a league away. Lilac and gooseberries. And something else. Something… broken.” Her jaw tightens. “And you smell like a corpse that forgot to lie down.” His grin widens. “Better.” They circle. She moves left. He moves right. The distance between them remains constant, an invisible thread neither will break first. “You’ve been killing,” she says. “The villages along the pass. You leave them drained, but not dead. Why?” “Why not?” He spreads his hands. “I am a monster. Monsters kill. It is what we do.” “You’re toying with them.” “I am *amusing* myself.” His voice drops, soft and dangerous. “There is a difference.” Yennefer stops. The spell in her palm shifts, ready to become fire or frost or something that will peel the flesh from his bones. “I could destroy you,” she says. Alucard laughs again, louder this time. The sound echoes off the stones, bounces between the trees. “Oh, I doubt that very much.” He moves. She does not see him cross the distance. One moment he is ten paces away, the next he is before her, close enough that she smells the grave dirt on his breath. Her spell lashes out—a blade of pure chaos—and slices through his throat. Black blood sprays. He does not stop grinning. The wound seals itself in a heartbeat, flesh knitting like thread through cloth. He touches his neck, looks at the blood on his fingers, and licks them clean. “Sharp,” he says. “But not sharp enough.” Yennefer teleports ten feet back, heart hammering. She has fought monsters. She has killed them. But this one—this one is *wrong*. The magic that animates him is ancient, chaotic, nothing like the structured necromancy she knows. “You are not a simple vampire,” she breathes. “Simple?” He sounds offended. “My dear sorceress. I have walked this earth for centuries. I have drunk the blood of kings and crushed the skulls of saints. I am Alucard. I am the night itself.” “You are a creature of hunger and pride,” she counters. “Nothing more.” His smile falters. Just for a moment. She sees it—the crack in his arrogance. “And you,” he says slowly, “are a woman who reshaped her own flesh to hide a deformity. A woman who sold her womb for power and now regrets the bargain.” The words hit like a blade between the ribs. Yennefer’s vision goes white. The spell that erupts from her is not measured, not controlled—it is raw, furious chaos that tears the ground between them, that shatters stone and scorches earth. When the dust clears, Alucard is gone. She spins, searching, and finds him perched on the watchtower above her, legs dangling like a child on a fence. “There she is,” he murmurs. “There is the fire.” She wants to kill him. She wants to tear him apart atom by atom. But she also wants—something else. Something she does not name. “Why are you here?” she demands. “What do you want?” Alucard regards her for a long moment. The red moon paints his face in blood tones. “I am looking for something,” he says. “A challenge. A worthy opponent. Someone who can make me *feel*.” “And you thought you found it in me?” “I thought I might.” He leaps down, landing silently. “But you are afraid. You hide behind your spells and your sharp tongue, but underneath, you are just another woman running from her own reflection.” Yennefer’s eyes narrow. “And you are just a monster playing at godhood. You hide behind your power because without it, you are nothing but a corpse that refuses to stay buried.” They stand facing each other. The wolves have begun to howl again, distant and mournful. Alucard removes his glasses. His eyes are crimson, ancient, burning. They hold centuries of slaughter and boredom and desperate, aching loneliness. “Perhaps,” he says quietly, “we are both running.” The admission hangs between them, fragile as spun glass. Yennefer does not lower her hands. But she does not attack. “What do you want, vampire?” He smiles, and for the first time, it does not look like a threat. “To see what you become when you stop running.” The moon bleeds overhead. The wolves howl on. Neither of them looks away.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a crossover fanfiction meeting the prompt's requirements: third person, present tense, roughly the requested length, medieval European setting, and the specified power dynamic between Alucard and Yennefer. Both characters are recognizable—Alucard's theatrical sadism, regeneration, and loneliness; Yennefer's sharp tongue, hidden deformity, and infertility wound. The dialogue crackles in places ("Did you lose your broom?" / "I lost my patience"), and the circling structure of the confrontation is well executed. Strengths: The prose is economical and atmospheric, with strong sensory grounding (copper and grave soil, the bleeding moon). The escalation from banter to violence to mutual recognition is well paced. Alucard's probing of Yennefer's infertility is a sharp, character-true beat, and her uncontrolled chaos blast in response is earned. The ending—two predators acknowledging shared flight—lands with appropriate ambiguity. Weaknesses: The piece leans on familiar beats: the "we're not so different" resolution is somewhat predictable, and Alucard's sudden vulnerability ("we are both running") arrives a touch quickly given how little Yennefer has actually demonstrated. His knowledge of her past (reshaped flesh, sold womb) is unexplained—convenient omniscience. Some lines verge on cliché ("I am the night itself"). The emotional complexity is gestured at rather than fully inhabited; Yennefer's "something she does not name" is told rather than shown. The strzyga setup is dropped without payoff. Still, the voice is consistent, the tone controlled, and the piece reads as competent, confident fanfiction with genuine moments of tension and wit. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 65.0
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The fluorescent lights of Green Dolphin Street Prison hum with a sickly pallor, casting long shadows across the concrete floor. Jolyne Cujoh leans against the wall of the exercise yard, her butterfly tattoo catching the light as she picks at a frayed thread on her jumpsuit. She’s been here long enough to know every guard’s footstep, every rat’s scuttle. But the woman who steps into the yard today is new. She’s auburn-haired, with ringed yellow eyes that gleam like traffic signals in fog. She wears a crisp suit, out of place among the orange jumpsuits and rusted barbed wire. A guard trails her, but his face is blank—slack-jawed, like a puppet with cut strings. The cameras above flicker, then go dark. Jolyne smirks. *Security’s always shitting itself around here.* “You’re Jolyne Cujoh,” the woman says. Her voice is syrup-sweet, soft as a lullaby. “I’m Makima. I’ve heard so much about your… ability.” Jolyne doesn’t move. “Yeah? And who the hell are you? New warden? Psychiatrist with a death wish?” Makima smiles. It doesn’t reach her eyes. “Something like that. I’m here to observe. To understand.” “Understand what?” Jolyne’s fingers twitch. A thread of string peels from her forearm, coiling like a serpent. “Your Stand.” Makima’s gaze drops to the string. “Stone Free. You unravel your body into threads. You control them with precision. It’s fascinating, really. The way you’ve adapted to this place.” She takes a step closer. “Most prisoners break. You’ve woven yourself into a weapon.” Jolyne’s jaw tightens. The string retracts. “You know about Stands? That’s not exactly public record.” “I know a lot of things.” Makima tilts her head. “I’m very good at making people tell me what I want.” A chill runs down Jolyne’s spine. It’s not the cold—it’s the way Makima says it. Like she’s discussing the weather. Like people are just… objects. “Let’s cut the crap,” Jolyne says, pushing off the wall. “You want something from me. Everyone in this shithole does. What is it? My Stand? My father’s connections?” Makima’s smile widens. “Your loyalty. You protect your friends. Your father. Even strangers, if they earn it. That’s rare.” She pauses. “I collect rare things.” “I’m not a thing,” Jolyne snaps. “And I’m not a dog you can leash.” Makima’s eyes flicker. For a second, Jolyne sees something ancient in them—a hunger, cold and bottomless. Then it’s gone. “Dogs are loyal because they choose to be. But they can be… redirected.” The air thickens. Jolyne feels it—a pressure, like someone’s pressing a thumb into her brain. *She’s trying to control me.* Her Stand responds instinctively, threads bursting from her skin, wrapping around her arms like armor. “Back off,” she growls. “I don’t know what kind of devil you are, but I’ve fought worse.” Makima doesn’t flinch. She simply watches, amused. “Devil? No. I’m human. Mostly.” She gestures to the dead cameras. “But I do have a gift for persuasion.” “You mean manipulation.” “Same thing, in the right hands.” Jolyne’s fingers curl into fists. The strings tighten. She’s ready to strike—to wrap Makima in a cocoon of razor-thin thread and squeeze until she talks. But something stops her. *She’s too calm. Too confident. This is a trap.* “You’re not here to observe,” Jolyne says slowly. “You’re here to test me. To see if I’m worth your time.” Makima’s smile finally reaches her eyes. It’s the most terrifying thing Jolyne has ever seen. “You’re smarter than you look, Jolyne. That’s good. Intelligence makes for a more interesting pet.” “I’ll kill you before I’m anyone’s pet.” “I know.” Makima turns, her heels clicking on the concrete. “That’s what makes this fun.” She walks away, and the cameras flicker back to life. The guard follows, still blank-faced. Jolyne watches her go, her heart hammering. *What the hell was that?* She doesn’t sleep that night. She sits in her cell, threading and unthreading her fingers, replaying the conversation. Makima’s words coil around her mind like her own strings. *Loyalty. Rare. Pet.* The woman is a predator wearing a human mask. And she’s interested in Jolyne. The next morning, a note is slipped under her door. It’s written in elegant script: *“Meet me in the chapel. I have a proposition. —M”* Jolyne crushes it in her fist. *Proposition my ass.* But she goes. Because if there’s one thing she’s learned from her father, it’s that you don’t run from a fight. You face it head-on, even if the enemy looks like a damn angel. The chapel is empty, save for Makima standing before the altar. She’s holding a leash. At the end of it is a guard—the same one from yesterday, now on his hands and knees, panting like a dog. “He was rude to you yesterday,” Makima says, not looking up. “I’ve corrected his behavior.” Jolyne’s stomach turns. “You’re insane.” “I’m efficient.” Makima drops the leash. The guard whimpers. “I want to make a contract with you, Jolyne. Your Stand in exchange for your freedom. I can get you out of this prison. I can give you anything you want.” “And what do you get?” “Your loyalty. Your power. You’ll serve me.” Jolyne laughs, bitter and sharp. “You think I’d sell myself out for a get-out-of-jail-free card? I’m not that desperate.” Makima’s eyes narrow. “Everyone has a price.” “Not me.” Jolyne’s strings erupt from her body, forming a web that fills the chapel. “And if you try to control me, I’ll wrap you so tight you’ll wish you’d never heard of Stone Free.” Makima doesn’t move. She simply watches, the smile returning. “We’ll see.” She steps past Jolyne, the guard scrambling to follow. “I have time. And I always get what I want.” She leaves Jolyne standing in the chapel, surrounded by her own threads, heart pounding. The cameras flicker again as Makima disappears down the hall. Jolyne knows this isn’t over. It’s only just begun. And for the first time in a long time, she’s genuinely afraid.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece fulfills the core assignment: third person, present tense, roughly the requested length, set at Green Dolphin Street Prison, with Jolyne suspicious of Makima and Makima intrigued by Stone Free. The escalating battle of wits is present, though it resolves into a fairly standard "contract offer refused" beat rather than anything genuinely dangerous or inventive. Strengths: The prose is clean and controlled, with a few effective images ("ringed yellow eyes that gleam like traffic signals in fog," the slack-jawed guard "like a puppet with cut strings"). Jolyne's voice is broadly right—foul-mouthed, defiant, quick to threaten. The chapel scene with the leashed guard is a good, economical use of Makima's established behavior. The pacing is brisk and the structure (yard confrontation, sleepless night, chapel proposition) is coherent. Weaknesses: The characterization leans on shorthand rather than depth. Jolyne's interiority is mostly stated ("She's genuinely afraid") rather than dramatized, and Makima is written as an archetypal smiling predator without the specific texture that makes her chilling in the source—the mimicry of warmth, the mundane politeness, the offhand cruelty framed as care. The dialogue is serviceable but exchanges like "You mean manipulation." / "Same thing, in the right hands." are snappy-clever without much surprise. Several stock phrases recur: "It doesn't reach her eyes," "heart pounding/hammering," "ancient hunger." The escalation promised by the prompt ("escalates dangerously") never truly materializes—Makima simply leaves twice, and the story ends on a declaration of future conflict rather than a payoff. Jolyne's final fear feels asserted rather than earned, since she has dominated every exchange. The ending is a cliffhanger-shaped shrug. Still, this is competent, readable fan fiction with no major incoherence, no purple excess, and reasonable fidelity to both characters' public-facing traits. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 74.5
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**SCP-XXXX - Temporal Correspondence Anomaly (Provisional)** **Researcher:** Dr. Elias Vance, Senior Researcher, Site-19 **Date of Initial Report:** 2024-03-12 **Subject:** Personal log, with appended anomalous notes. --- I found the first note on a Tuesday. It was tucked under my keyboard, written in my own handwriting—a cramped, left-slanting script I’d recognize anywhere. The paper was standard Foundation bond, slightly yellowed at the edges. The message was simple: *“Elias—do not approve the 4-7 transfer. The 682 test is a trap. Trust no one from Level 4 Logistics. —E.V.”* I laughed. I had no pending transfer for SCP-682. The test schedule for March was blank. I crumpled it, tossed it in the shredder, and went back to my coffee. But I kept the scrap, just in case. Old habits. The second note appeared three days later, on my desk at 14:32. I was in the middle of a containment review for SCP-173. The security cameras in my office are hardwired and monitored by Site Command. I saw the timestamp on the feed: 14:31:59, my desk is empty. 14:32:00, the note is there, flat and centered, as if placed by a ghost. The feed glitched for exactly 0.4 seconds—a black frame, then back to normal. The glitch is now a documented signature event. That note read: *“They’re in the vents. You have 48 hours. Tell O5-7. He’ll believe you. —E.V.”* I didn’t tell O5-7. I told my supervisor, Dr. Chen. She ordered a psychological evaluation and a memetic screening. Negative. No anomalous influence. No brain tumors. I started to wonder if I was losing my mind. --- The notes accelerated. They came daily, then hourly. They were always in my handwriting, always on that same yellowed paper. The content grew desperate, fractured. I began to recognize the signs of acute stress in my own prose—the erratic punctuation, the misspellings I never made. *“No no no they lied about the recontainment the red door is not a door it’s a mouth and it’s ALREADY OPEN why won’t you listen I am you I am screaming from inside the breach and you are just sitting there drinking your tea”* I was drinking tea when I read that. I stopped. I stared at the note. The words *“the red door is not a door”* were underlined three times. But there is no red door in Site-19. I checked the architectural blueprints. I checked the SCP-001 proposals. Nothing. Dr. Chen put me on administrative leave. She assigned a containment specialist, Dr. Rourke, to monitor my office remotely. The cameras glitched every time a new note appeared. Rourke’s team ran a temporal anomaly sweep. The results were inconclusive—localized chroniton fluctuations within a 0.5-meter radius of my desk, but no clear source. The fluctuations matched no known SCP signature. Then the notes began to contradict reality. *“The breach is in 6 hours. The entity is SCP-████. It wears Chen’s face. Do not trust her smile.”* SCP-████ does not exist. I checked the database. I checked the Foundation’s internal archives. No such designation. I asked Dr. Chen about it. She smiled—a perfectly normal, concerned smile—and said, “Elias, you need rest. This is stress.” I wanted to believe her. But the note had said *“Do not trust her smile.”* I started to wonder: was the future me lying? Or was the present me being gaslit by something wearing my friend’s face? --- On the fifth day, I found a note that broke me. *“I am not your future. I am a copy. The real you died in the first breach. I am writing this from a timeline that should not exist. The Foundation is not trying to stop the breach. They are trying to contain the knowledge of it. They are afraid of what you will remember. Chen is not Chen. She is a narrative. A story told by the red door. The red door is not a door. It is a recursion. It is a lie that became true. I am sorry. I am so sorry. I am writing this with my own blood now because the pen ran out and the paper is the only thing that is real and even it is not real. The cameras are not cameras. They are eyes. They are watching you read this. They are watching you doubt. Do not doubt. Doubt is the door. Doubt is the mouth. Doubt is how they enter.”* The note was written in red ink. I checked my pen drawer. All black. I checked my hands. Clean. No cuts, no blood. But the note smelled like copper. I called Dr. Chen. She arrived in six minutes. I showed her the note. She read it, her face unreadable. Then she said, “Elias, this is clearly a psychological manipulation. We have a candidate. SCP-2747, the Memetic Annihilator, has been known to project false temporal narratives into vulnerable personnel. You were exposed during the 2022 containment review.” I nodded. It made sense. It was a textbook explanation. But I remembered something from the note: *“Chen is not Chen. She is a narrative.”* I looked at her. Really looked. Her smile was symmetrical. Her eyes were the right shade of brown. She blinked at the correct intervals. But there was something off about the way she stood. Too still. Too centered. As if she were a photograph of herself. I said, “Okay. I’ll take the leave.” She patted my shoulder. Her hand was warm. It felt real. I went home. I locked my office. I checked the cameras—they were still glitching, every few seconds now. I sat at my desk and waited for the next note. It hasn’t come yet. But I can hear something in the vents. A scratching. A whisper. It sounds like my own voice, repeating the same phrase over and over: *“The red door is open. The red door is open. The red door is open.”* I’m not sure if I should call Dr. Chen. I’m not sure if she’s real. I’m not sure if I am. I’m writing this report on paper. The same yellowed bond. The same left-slanting script. I don’t remember starting it. But the words are in my handwriting, and they keep coming. I think I’m the one writing the notes now. I think I’m the future self. And I think the breach has already happened. —Dr. Elias Vance, 2024-03-17, 03:47 AM **Addendum:** The above report was found on Dr. Vance’s desk at 04:12 AM. He was not present. The security footage shows him writing it, then looking up at the camera, mouthing the words “I’m sorry,” and walking out of frame. The red door in his office—which does not exist in the building plans—is now visible on the feed. It remains closed. Site Command has initiated a reality-anchoring field around Dr. Vance’s office. The door has not opened. The notes have stopped. Dr. Chen is still smiling.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, well-executed SCP piece that hits nearly all prompt requirements: first-person researcher perspective, past tense, escalating incoherent notes, contradictory information, Foundation investigation into temporal vs. psychological causes, and the researcher's eroding self-trust. The structure—log entries interspersed with the notes themselves—is exactly what the prompt requested. Strengths: The escalation is well-paced, from a mundane first note to the blood-written fifth note. The camera glitch as a "documented signature event" is a nice procedural detail that grounds the anomaly in SCP verisimilitude. The red door motif works as an effective recurring image, and the final addendum—Vance mouthing "I'm sorry" and walking out of frame, the door now visible but closed, "Dr. Chen is still smiling"—lands a genuinely chilling ending. The twist that Vance may now be the one writing the notes is earned by the escalating logic of the piece. The Foundation's competing explanations (temporal sweep vs. SCP-2747 memetic manipulation) fulfill the prompt's requirement for institutional ambiguity. Weaknesses: Some elements are familiar to the point of cliché—"I'm not sure if she's real. I'm not sure if I am" is a well-worn horror beat, and the "entity wearing someone's face" trope is standard. The prose occasionally tells rather than shows ("That note broke me," "The content grew desperate, fractured"). Dr. Chen's dialogue is functional but a bit flat and expository ("You were exposed during the 2022 containment review"). The "narrative/story told by the red door" meta-conceit flirts with overwrought self-reference, though it mostly stays controlled. The word count is roughly on target. The ending's darkness is earned by the buildup, and the final line is an effective closer rather than an incongruous positivity problem. Overall, this is competent, engaging, professional-grade SCP fiction with a few predictable beats but a strong finish. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 69.8
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-XXXX **Object Class:** Keter **Special Containment Procedures:** Foundation personnel embedded within municipal building inspection and demolition agencies are to report any instances of unmarked doors found in structurally isolated sections of condemned or abandoned structures. Mobile Task Force Mu-4 ("Debuggers") is to be dispatched to any reported location to verify the presence of SCP-XXXX. Upon confirmation, the building is to be immediately sealed under the guise of structural instability. No personnel are to enter SCP-XXXX without Level 5/XXXX clearance. All recovered documentation is to be stored in a dedicated, fireproof archive at Site-01 under continuous surveillance. **Description:** SCP-XXXX is the collective designation for a series of identical, unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide. Each instance is constructed of plain, unvarnished oak with a simple brass knob. No hinges, keyholes, or manufacturer’s marks are present. In complete darkness, a faint, cold glow escapes through the door’s edges, described by observers as "the color of old bone." The door cannot be opened by any means other than turning the knob; any attempt to force it or cut through it results in the door vanishing and reappearing in a different location within the same structure. When opened, SCP-XXXX leads to a single, shared space: a massive archive of impossible dimensions. The interior is a single, windowless chamber estimated to be at least 300 meters in height, with walls receding into a faint, grey haze. The floor, ceiling, and walls are composed of a smooth, dark grey stone that does not match any known geological material. The space is filled with shelf units of the same stone, arranged in a grid pattern that extends beyond visual range. Each shelf is packed with bound volumes, scrolls, and loose folios, all written in a script that is a direct linguistic ancestor to modern English, Russian, Mandarin, and Arabic. The archive contains a complete historical record of a global civilization that predates any known human society by approximately 12,000 years. This civilization, designated "Civilization-1," possessed technology and social structures comparable to the late 20th century, but with a unified global government. The final entries in their records describe a catastrophic containment failure at a facility they called the "Custodial Vault." The failure is described not as an explosion, but as a "leak" of a "conceptual pathogen" that caused all human knowledge of the civilization to be erased from reality. The archive itself was built as a "hard copy" backup, hidden in a pocket dimension. Of greatest concern to the Foundation: the archive contains references to the SCP Foundation under a different name—the **"Society for the Preservation of Reality."** Personnel files for current Foundation staff, including O5 Council members, are present, dated with timestamps corresponding to the era of Civilization-1. These files contain detailed psychometric profiles, family histories, and photographs of individuals who are alive today. The implication is that the current Foundation is a re-formation of the Society after the collapse of Civilization-1. **Exploration Log XXXX-Alpha-7:** **Date:** 2024-03-14 **Team:** MTF Mu-4 ("Debuggers") - Lead Researcher Dr. Helena Vance, Agent K. Reyes, Agent T. Miller **Objective:** Recovery of documentation from Sector 7-Gamma. Team entered SCP-XXXX at 14:32. Standard silence protocol observed. Dr. Vance noted the ambient temperature was a constant 12°C, with no detectable air currents. The team moved through rows of shelves, following a pre-mapped route to Sector 7-Gamma. At 14:47, Agent Reyes signaled a halt. He reported hearing a rhythmic scraping sound, like metal on stone, approximately 50 meters ahead. The team advanced slowly. Through a gap in the shelves, they observed three figures. The figures were humanoid but wore full-body suits of a material resembling thick, white rubber. Their helmets were featureless, with a single, dark visor. They were systematically removing books from a section of shelving and placing them into large, black plastic crates. The crates were already sealed with a red wax stamp bearing an unfamiliar sigil: a circle bisected by a vertical line. Dr. Vance ordered the team to observe. Agent Miller attempted to take a photograph. The flash from his camera, despite being set to no-flash mode, triggered a reaction. The figures stopped moving. In unison, they turned their helmeted heads toward the team. They did not attack. They simply gathered their crates and walked away, with a brisk, unhurried pace, disappearing into the grey haze of the far wall. The scraping sound faded. The team approached the now-empty section. On the floor, a single document had been dropped. It was a personnel file. **Recovered Document Excerpt - File #O5-01-7G:** > **Subject:** O5-1 > **Designation:** The Custodian of the First Gate > **Previous Incarnation:** Director of Containment, Society for the Preservation of Reality, Vault Site-01 > **Notes:** Subject displays a recurring pattern of unauthorized visits to the Archive. Time-stamped access logs from the Vault's primary interface show Subject entering Sector 7-Gamma on three separate occasions during the final 72 hours before the Vault's failure. Subject was observed removing specific files related to "Containment Protocols for Unstable Conceptual Entities" and "Procedures for Civilization-Reset." No records of these files have been found in the Archive since. The Society's Internal Affairs division has flagged this activity as "High Concern." Recommendation: Subject is to be considered a potential vector for the leak. **Addendum XXXX-01:** O5-1 has refused to comment on the contents of the recovered file. A review of Foundation internal access logs from the past decade confirms that O5-1 has logged into the Foundation's deep archive database from remote terminals on dates that correlate with the timestamps on the recovered file. No official mission orders or debriefings exist for these sessions. The file was found in a section of the Archive that is actively being emptied by the white-suited entities. The Foundation does not know who these entities are, why they are removing the records, or what they intend to do with them. The Archive is shrinking.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry hits all the required prompt elements: identical unmarked doors in abandoned buildings, an architecturally impossible archive, references to a prior global civilization destroyed by a containment failure, the Foundation appearing under a different name ("Society for the Preservation of Reality"), personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago, hazmat-like entities removing sections who flee when approached, and evidence of unauthorized O5 visits. The format follows SCP conventions well—object class, containment procedures, description, exploration log, recovered document, addendum. Strengths: The prose is clean, clinical, and appropriately restrained for the SCP format. The "conceptual pathogen" leak is a nice touch, as is the detail that the door vanishes when forced. The recovered O5-1 file is the strongest element—it reframes the Foundation's own leadership as a potential vector for the previous collapse, and the addendum's final line ("The Archive is shrinking") lands with genuine dread. The hazmat entities' behavior—turning in unison, then simply leaving—is understated and effective. Weaknesses: The piece is somewhat mechanical in its execution, ticking boxes rather than building atmosphere. The exploration log is thin—mostly summary rather than moment-to-moment tension, with minimal dialogue or sensory detail beyond temperature. The team's emotional reactions are absent; they could be anyone. The "Society for the Preservation of Reality" name is functional but unsurprising. The word count falls short of the 1000-word seed (~850). The civilization's script being an ancestor to four major world languages is a hand-wave. Some elements (the red wax sigil) are introduced without payoff, though that's forgivable in SCP format. The ending is appropriately dark and earned, though the piece never achieves real emotional complexity—it's a competent exercise rather than a haunting one. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 71.8
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The air of New Thebes tasted of salt and something else—a metallic tang, like ozone after a storm, but sweeter. The official briefings had called it “atmospheric particulate,” a euphemism for the biogenic dust of a world that did not wish to be breathed. Envoy Corin Vesper had read the reports. They had not prepared him for the weight of it in his lungs. He slipped out of the Consulate through a service entrance at the seventeenth hour, when the shift changed and the guards were more concerned with their own relief than with the movements of a junior diplomat. The streets of the port district were not the sanitized thoroughfares shown in the orientation holos. Those had been wide, clean, lined with the geometric facades of administrative buildings. Here, the architecture had grown organically, like a coral reef—tiered balconies of fired clay and recycled polymer, strung with vines that bore fruit the color of bruises. The air was thick with steam from open cookfires and the low, rhythmic hum of a language that had drifted far from its Terran root. Vesper walked slowly. He was tall for an Earth-born, but here he felt gangly, unfinished. The people of New Thebes were shorter, denser, their bones heavier to withstand the planet’s higher gravity. Their skin had taken on a deep, coppery patina, a response to the high levels of ultraviolet radiation that the briefing had described as “manageable with standard shielding.” No one here used shielding. Their eyes were large, dark, set wide apart—a trait that had emerged in the last four centuries, an adaptation for the perpetual twilight of the planet’s long, cloud-choked days. The market was a chaos of color and scent. Stalls overflowed with handwoven fabrics, their dyes a spectrum Vesper had no name for. There was a blue that seemed to absorb light rather than reflect it, a green that shimmered with a faint, internal luminescence, a red so deep it felt like a wound. He reached out to touch a bolt of cloth, and the vendor—a woman whose face was a map of fine, radial wrinkles—caught his wrist with surprising strength. Her grip was warm, calloused. “Offworlder,” she said, not a question. Her accent was thick, the vowels flattened. “You want to buy, you look with eyes. You touch, you owe.” Vesper pulled his hand back, offering a placating gesture. “I apologize. The fabric is beautiful. I’ve never seen dyes like these.” She studied him, her large eyes unblinking. “You wouldn’t have. Earth colors are thin. They come from rocks and bugs. These come from the deep-fungus. You have to go to the caves, three days north. You have to trade your own weight in salt for the right to harvest it.” She released his wrist and turned back to her wares. “You wouldn’t last a day in the caves.” He bought a small square of the luminescent green, a transaction that involved a complex negotiation of gestures and a coin he did not recognize. The coin was accepted, but with a look that suggested he had overpaid. He did not care. He was learning. For two hours he walked, observing. He saw no uniformed officials, no visible enforcers of the Colonial Compact. He saw children playing a game with weighted stones, their laughter sharp and unguarded. He saw an old man repairing a solar panel with tools that looked hand-forged, his movements precise, unhurried. He saw a couple arguing in a doorway, their voices rising and falling in a rhythm that sounded almost musical. There was a texture to this society, a lived-in quality that the briefings had flattened into statistics and risk assessments. The briefings had spoken of “cultural friction” and “resource allocation disputes.” They had not mentioned the smell of the cookfires, or the way the children’s laughter made the air feel lighter. When he returned to the Consulate, the shift had changed again. The guard at the service entrance was new, and she did not look relieved. She looked at him with the cold, assessing gaze of a professional. “Envoy Vesper. Command is waiting.” The reprimand was delivered by a woman named Yarrow, the station’s Chief of Protocol. She did not raise her voice. She did not need to. Her eyes were the color of steel, and her words were clipped, precise, like the snap of a bone. “You were not authorized for unescorted movement. You were not briefed for unescorted movement. The local population has not been stabilized for diplomatic engagement. You have compromised your own security and the security of this mission.” Vesper stood with his hands clasped behind his back, his face neutral. He had been trained for this. “I observed no threat, Chief. The people were… ordinary.” “Ordinary is a luxury you do not have,” Yarrow said. “You are an offworlder. You are a symbol. Every interaction you have is a negotiation, whether you intend it or not. Your little walk has been noted. The Minister of Science has requested a meeting.” Vesper’s pulse quickened. The Minister of Science was a political posting, not a scientific one. The current officeholder, a man named Aldric Venn, was a relic of the old Earth administration, a bureaucrat who had been stationed on New Thebes for thirty years. He was said to be the power behind the Governor’s chair. “When?” Vesper asked. “Now.” The Minister’s office was not in the administrative wing. It was a low, domed structure at the edge of the compound, built from the same fired clay as the market stalls. The walls were lined with shelves of data crystals and physical books—a deliberate anachronism. Venn sat behind a desk that was bare except for a single, unlit lamp. He was a thin man, his skin pale and papery, untouched by the deep copper of the locals. His hair was white, his eyes a watery blue. He looked like a ghost. “Sit,” Venn said, without looking up. He was reading a paper document, his fingers tracing the lines. “You went into the city.” “Yes.” “And what did you see?” Vesper took a breath. He chose his words carefully. “I saw a society that is more complex than the briefings suggest. I saw people who are self-sufficient, resourceful, and deeply distrustful of us.” Venn looked up. His smile was thin, without warmth. “Good. The briefings are lies. They have to be. You can’t govern a colony with truth; you govern with narrative.” He set the paper down. “You’re young. You have ideals. You think that understanding will lead to peace. It won’t. Understanding leads to choice, and choice leads to conflict. Your job, Envoy, is not to understand. Your job is to manage the conflict so that it does not break the Compact.” Vesper felt the weight of the man’s gaze, the long years of compromise and calculation. “And if the conflict is already breaking the Compact?” Venn’s smile widened, a crack in the porcelain. “Then you will learn what it means to be an offworlder. You are not one of them. You are not one of us. You are a thing in between, a tool. The question is: who will wield you?”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, professional piece of genre fiction that hits all the prompt's beats: the unauthorized walk, the market encounter, the reprimand, and the testing conversation with the Minister. The prose is controlled and economical, with some genuinely strong sensory details—the "biogenic dust of a world that did not wish to be breathed," the bruise-colored fruit, the vendor's "You touch, you owe." The Le Guin influence shows in the anthropological patience of the market scene and the thematic interest in what "offworlder" means as a category of person. Strengths: The worldbuilding is delivered through observation rather than exposition dumps; the physical divergence of the colonists is shown concretely (gravity-adapted bodies, coppery skin, wide-set eyes). The Venn scene has a decent cynical thesis—"you govern with narrative"—and the closing line ("who will wield you?") lands as an effective hook, if a slightly melodramatic one. Weaknesses: The piece is heavily familiar. The wise-elder-political-operator-who-mentors/tests-the-young-envoy is stock; Venn speaks in aphorisms that feel written rather than spoken ("Understanding leads to choice, and choice leads to conflict"). The vendor scene, while pleasant, is a well-worn trope—the streetwise local who teaches the naive offworlder. Characters are archetypes: Vesper is a blank everyman whose "ideals" are asserted rather than demonstrated; Yarrow is a stern functionary; Venn is a ghostly schemer. The emotional register stays cool throughout—appropriate to the style, but the piece never surprises or unsettles the way Le Guin's best work does. The ending is a setup for a longer work rather than a satisfying chapter in itself. Some phrasing strains slightly ("like the snap of a bone," "a crack in the porcelain"). The dialogue is serviceable but rarely distinctive; Venn's lines are the strongest, Vesper's the flattest. There is no meandering, no purple excess, no tonal inconsistency. It is solid, readable, and somewhat safe. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 71.2
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The mushrooms were a lie, of course. A pretty, bioluminescent lie that had outlived the company that designed them. They pulsed a soft, chemical cyan from the grout lines of the cracked lab tiles, feeding on the spilled nutrient broth and the broken dreams of a dozen dead biotech firms. Kael ignored them. They were useless. You couldn’t eat a lie. His own breath fogged in the chill of the old GeneSys Annex. The building’s climate control had died with the grid, but the emergency backup—a jury-rigged Stirling engine running off a methane digester in the basement—kept the cold storage at a grudging four degrees Celsius. It was enough. Just barely. He called it the “Thermal Crucible.” It was a repurposed PCR machine, its lid held shut with a strip of salvaged conveyor belt and a ratchet strap. The heating block was pitted from years of abuse, and the optical sensor was a cheap photodiode he’d glued to the lid with epoxy. It wasn’t precise. It wasn’t clean. But it could copy a strand of DNA before the damn thing fell apart. That was the problem. The whole world was falling apart, one generation at a time. The Old World’s sin had been elegance. Every seed, every crop, every vitamin-producing gut bacteria had been designed with a kill switch. A single generation of viability. You bought the patent, you grew the crop, you harvested the fruit, and the seeds were sterile. Next year, you bought more. It was a perfect, recurring revenue stream. Until the supply chains snapped. Until the corporate states collapsed into a dozen squabbling fiefdoms. Now, the only corn that grew was the stuff Kael could splice from salvaged, degrading templates. He had a contract. A good one. The Red Hill settlement needed a blight-resistant potato. Their old stock had rotted in the ground, a victim of a gene-drive fungus that had been designed to kill a competitor’s product and had never been recalled. The pay was a liter of medical-grade ethanol—pure enough for the sterilizer—and a promise of first harvest shares. Kael’s hands trembled as he pipetted the master mix into the thin-walled tubes. The tremor wasn’t from cold. It was from the splice. Three weeks ago, he’d taken a job that paid in medicine. A child with a failing liver. The only cure was a set of modified hepatocytes, but the old gene therapies were locked in proprietary formats no one could read. So Kael had done the only thing he could. He’d spliced a patch from a fast-regenerating earthworm into the child’s own cells. The kid was alive. Kael’s own liver, however, had started producing a strange, waxy enzyme that made his urine glow faintly under UV light. It was a side effect. An unexpected upside, the kid’s mother had called it, when she saw the glowing sample. “He’ll never get lost in the dark.” The upside was that his hands shook less now when he was tired. The downside was that he was always tired. He loaded the Thermal Crucible. The ratchet strap groaned. He pressed the start button—a salvaged doorbell switch wired into the microcontroller. The machine hummed, clicked, and began its cycle. Denature. Anneal. Extend. Over and over, copying a fragment of a potato’s genome, trying to stitch in a blight-resistance gene from a wild relative that had been sequenced before the Fall. While it ran, Kael checked his other tools. The gel electrophoresis rig was a repurposed aquarium, with platinum wire electrodes he’d pulled from a junkyard catalytic converter. The power supply was a car battery and a voltage regulator he’d salvaged from a dead solar inverter. It wasn’t pretty, but it worked. He’d stained the gel with a homemade ethidium bromide substitute—a fluorescent protein he’d extracted from the lab’s own glowing mushrooms. The mushrooms were a lie, but they were a useful lie. The machine beeped. He released the strap, hissing as the hot lid seared his fingertips. He didn’t flinch. The nerve damage from the third splice had been a gift. No more pain. No more feeling in his right hand at all. He ran the gel. The bands were faint, but they were there. A clean insertion. The potato would grow. It would fruit. And the seeds would be sterile. He couldn’t fix that. No one could. The kill switches were too deep, too fundamental. Every generation, the genetic clock ticked down to zero. The only way to keep a crop alive was to keep splicing, keep copying, keep burning through the degraded templates until they were nothing but noise. He bottled the amplified DNA, labeling it with a Sharpie on a scrap of duct tape. *Red Hill – Blight Resistant – Batch 4.* He’d need to deliver it by dusk. The settlement had a courier who ran the wasteland on foot, carrying vials in a padded vest. Kael had paid for that vest with two fingers. A fair trade. As he sealed the vial, his right hand began to ache. A dull, thrumming pain that crawled up his forearm. The nerve damage was healing. That was the other unexpected upside. His body was adapting. The worm splice was mutating, integrating, becoming something new. He wasn’t sure if that was good or terrifying. He looked down at the glowing mushrooms. They were a lie, but they were a persistent lie. They’d been spliced to glow for a single season. That was three years ago. They’d adapted. They’d found a way. Maybe he could, too. He pocketed the vial, grabbed his coat, and stepped out into the cold, dead air of the world he was trying to feed. The black market contract was fulfilled. The settlement would have its potatoes. And Kael would have his ethanol, his shares, and one more day to figure out how to make the next generation last.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent, atmospheric biopunk chapter that hits nearly all prompt requirements: post-apocalyptic obsolescence-driven genetic engineering, a biohacker protagonist, jury-rigged lab equipment (ratcheted PCR machine, aquarium gel rig, catalytic converter electrodes), physical tolls and ironic upsides of self-experimentation (glowing urine, nerve damage as "gift," healing mutation), and a black market contract as the plot spine. The "mushrooms were a lie" framing device is effective, bookending the piece with a thematic resonance about adaptation and persistence. Strengths: the worldbuilding is economical and specific; the prose is controlled and mostly clean; the tone is consistently grim but wry; the details of salvaged equipment feel researched rather than hand-waved. The kill-switch premise is clearly articulated without infodump fatigue. Weaknesses: the character is a familiar archetype (self-sacrificing wasteland tinkerer with a tragic past implied through body horror), and the plot beats are predictable—contract, complication, fulfillment, hopeful note. The physical toll elements occasionally feel like a checklist of body-horror tropes rather than organic consequences; the "paid for that vest with two fingers" line is tossed off without context, which is evocative but borders on gratuitous edginess. The ending's hopeful turn ("Maybe he could, too") is slightly convenient, though the mushroom setup earns it reasonably well. Some minor logic wobble: nerve damage described as total numbness, then a "dull thrumming pain" in the same hand two paragraphs later—though this is framed as healing, it reads slightly inconsistent. There is no dialogue, so that criterion is excluded. Length is roughly on target (~1000 words). Overall: a solid, professional piece with good atmosphere and competent craft, lacking the originality or emotional depth of a standout work.
